Eskom cracks

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A crack and then a collapse - can Eskom keep the lights on as it scrambles to fix a collapsed coal silo

Summary:
A ten thousand ton coal silo at Majuba cracked and then collapsed 40 minutes later. Its a setback the country cannot afford. What went wrong - was this just an accident or is Eskoms lack of maintenance catching up with it. In 2008 rolling mass black outs cost thousands of jobs and was a major set back for the economy- are we seeing a repeat of those dark days again?

Further information:
Eskom breaks again Proposal

On Saturday around midday Eskom employees noticed a crack in one of Majuba’s coal silos. Less than an hour later this enormous structure had collapsed sending staff into a tailspin and the country into stage 2 load shedding less than 12 hours later.

On Sunday the new CEO Tshediso Matona and his team convened a hasty press conference and apologized to the nation. 12 pages of load shedding schedules were released and trucks lined up outside Majuba to deliver coal manually to save South Africa’s grid

# Load shedding became the trending topic across TWITTER SA as South Africans in towns and suburbs across the country vented their fury in the dark.

By Monday evening Andrew Etzinger Eskom’s Duracell communication man sounded more upbeat and it seemed that although things were bad they were not as catastrophic as Ted Blom had predicted. This release came from the Media desk:

Eskom is not load shedding today and does not anticipate that there will be any load shedding tomorrow as additional units have been returned from maintenance. If customers experience power outages during this period, we advise that they contact their electricity providers as it could be a localised problem.

The risk of load shedding has reduced significantly and the prognosis for the week is better than expected. The system will be under extreme pressure on Wednesday and Thursday as the water reserves that we built up over the weekend for our peaking plants will be depleted.

Eskom is pleased to announce that work at Majuba Power Station has progressed better than anticipated. Teams have worked non-stop since the incident on Saturday and have been able to connect coal feeder units which have enabled us to ramp up the supply from 600MW to 1 200 MW.

But that was only on Monday.

So what went wrong – Eskom say they will need to do a forensic investigation but Solidarity were less forgiving. On Monday afternoon they released this statement:

“Since January, Eskom has been aware of structural problems of the silo which collapsed at its Majuba power station the day before yesterday….Solidarity blames Eskom for not having addressed the issue, accusing the company of negligence. Solidarity has learnt that Eskom workers had been monitoring resonances at the silo since January. It had been reported to the company at that stage that, based on the increase in vibration, the silo was showing signs of deterioration.

According to Deon Reyneke, Solidarity’s Head of the Energy Industry, it was found in June this year, and again three weeks prior to the collapse, that the silo’s vibration had worsened. “Vibration of a concrete structure is extremely problematic. The vibration caused or worsened weaknesses in the silo and as the vibration increased, it eventually led to the collapse,” Reyneke explains.

But Eskom has disputed this and say that Solidarity has it all wrong.
Meanwhile we are told from both inside and outside Eskom that it could take anything from 3 months to a year to fix the problem.

Considering that Eskom is battling to keep the lights on without this latest collapse all bets are off on what the country could face in the upcoming summer.

Since 2008 there is nothing that angers people more than load- shedding. But anger is one thing – the effects on the economy are dramatic and we simply cannot afford another disaster like this. Azar Jammine explains how this latest Eskom collapse will impact on SA INC.

ESKOM CRACKS: viewing 1

AMALIA:
1. You say Anton Eberhart broke it on twitter we don’t know who he is – explain who he is
2. You need to clarify what is in the pics showing no maintenance – are these material things that are not fixed and how long have they been broken? Please add that in where you show those pictures - we need much more context.
3. You use the pics showing no maintenance twice and done explain which station they are from.
4. Explain clearly about the metal on metal rollers... and write it very carefully so that you are not implying that this is what caused the silo to collapse at Majuba.
5. SOLIDARITY GUY: Can you explain a little on the resonance he refers to - where did the resonance come from? What should the resonance be? what is resonance?
6. YOUR SOURCE : have we hidden his identity enough? he was happy with being shown in the wide
7. Where is Tony Smith based? Can you add that in?
8. Take out derek’s link about the 2008 interview.
9. We need another viewing tomorrow 12h30 at GM’s house.

NOZIPHO
1. The big thing that we cannot say is around the foregoing maintenance to chase bonuses. We have no proof of this its hearsay... to be fair comment has to be based on facts that are substantially true. Mention the R60mn bonuses. But you can’t say they are foregoing maintenance to get bonuses. Derek’s link and the confidential source are the problem... take out Derek’s link... reword it all.

2. N: Deon says Eskom knew and Eskom responds to say he is speaking about the wrong silo? would he give his source to you should we go before BCCSA? J: he says he can prove it.

3. You say Eskom admits they haven’t done maintenance for 4 years. What is the industry practice? Should it be every year or every two years. Have they been lax or is it normal? Its not clear that you are talking across the board. Sounds like its at Majuba. Also what is normal? You say they inspected the silo months ago. Joy: i will quote from the previous CEO’s letter where he refers to the lack of maintenance. N: be careful of context linking collapse of the silo to the maintenance issue... in the mind of the reasonable viewer 4 years will stick and people will think ‘no wonder it collapsed’. You need to change this.

4. TUTUKA station – the visuals we have don’t make sense. What are we seeing? Can you have an expert speaking about what we are seeing? Please give more context.

5. Take out Derek’s link entirely where he says they won’t talk to us because of the 2008 interview.

Press Release:


Eskom Cracks
Hours after Coal Silo 20 collapsed last weekend at Majuba Power Station headlines screamed imminent black outs. Against the odds Eskom pulled out all the stops to keep the lights on this week. But will they stay on? Carte Blanche goes to the coal face and uncovers serious allegations of inadequate maintenance.


Script:


Eskom Cracks Final Script TX 9th November 9, 2014.

Commentary one
Majuba power station, Mpumalanga On a good day it gives us 10 % of our electricity needs. Then last Saturday- a disaster

You tube video with up- sound

At 12 30 a crack appeared in Silo 20. Forty-five minutes later it collapsed.

Commentary Two
Expect serious load- shedding tweeted Energy expert, professor Anton Eberhard

LINK
Chris Yelland picked up on the tweets – the silo had collapsed at lunchtime but on Saturday evening Eskom were still trying to spin it differently

Chris Yelland Managing Director ee publishers
The executive team had been on site on Saturday afternoon, they knew that the silo had collapsed and they issued an approved press release in which it wasn’t mentioned – it simply mentioned there was a crack

Commentary Three
Some crack! Tweeted professor Eberhard, as the first pictures of the collapse went public. Engineer Chris Yelland explains what happened.

Chris Yelland
This central silo collapsed taking down with it the two incoming conveyers and the two feeder conveyers which means that no coal coming from the stock yard can reach the three silos – once the coal in those three silo’s runs out, then the power station has to shut down

Commentary Four
For new CEO Tshediso Matona it was a baptism by fire. At a hastily convened press conference a day later Eskom’s Dr Steve Lennon apologized.

Up Sound Dr Steve Lennon Eskom group executive Sustainabity
Any inconvenience is deeply regretted

Eskom could no longer hide the facts, as once again the awful spectre of load shedding faced the country.

Up sound Generator

Commentary five
As anger and generator sales went up, small businesses like Thys and Nadia’s salon had to fork out money they could ill afford

Thys
We have just started it for 5 minutes and our show room is filled with smoke and massive noise and people are coming here trying to relax and there is this noisy thing

Commentary six
Nothing provokes anger like load shedding. Small business owner Nandi Labuschagne is not impressed either

Nandi
I read through the media how many guys get these massive bonuses and I think really!!

Commentary Seven
She says load shedding will cripple her sand blasting business. Nandi employs eleven people. A generator will mean less money to employ others.

Nandi
Quotations I have here are ranging from R160 to R170 thousand. I can’t afford it right now

Commentary Eight
Azar Jammine says strikes led to small and medium enterprises that really add loadshedding and small businesses take the knock.

Azar Jammine
There have been some signs of recovery and an improvement and just as we are starting to assume a little more confidence and optimism we are now just lumbered with the possibility of load shedding anew

Commentary Nine
This year South Africa barely grew at all, limping along at 1.4%.



Chris Yelland
It’s costing the economy 75 rand per kw/h – well the cost that we pay is about R1 rand per kw/hour, so you can see that the damage to the economy is seventy five times higher than not having electricity.

Commentary ten
Eskom’s investigation will take 3- 6 months. What is known is that a year ago the silo was inspected.

CHRIS TITLE
It was found that there was nothing seriously wrong with it and it did not pose a significant risk – well one year later it collapsed and there is a reason for it – it didn’t just collapse!

LINK
Then on Monday Solidarity dropped a bombshell – They said Eskom had known about dangerous vibrations silo since January and they accused Eskom of negligence

Commentary eleven
Deon Reyneke is head of industry for the energy sector at the trade union.

Deon
Since January this year this whole problem was under the attention of Eskom it was reported to Eskom continuously that there was a problem with this Silo

Commentary Twelve
Eskom says Solidarity is confusing this silo with another one in the coal stockyard that was decommissioned

Deon
Eskom will try and confuse the public…. but I am not confused

Commentary thirteen
Eskom has admitted that across their fleet they are not doing sufficient maintenance. So was the collapse a construction problem or rather a lack of maintenance?

Deon
Well our members say its bad maintenance, preventative maintenance and no maintenance at all


LINK
Eskom have strenuously denied Solidarity’s claims but we were told by sources that there is a lack of maintenance on several of the power stations

Commentary fourteen
These screeching rollers under the conveyer belt leading to a silo at Thutuka power station have not been maintained.

Evan
The rollers grinding metal-to-metal, and that causes vibration to the silo. It runs 24 hours a day so that heat is so excessive! And then if there is a coal spillage ..that is a big fire hazard

Commentary fifteen
Our source who works at a power station says Eskom incentivize, cost cutting which results in skimping on maintenance.

Evan
Eskom management of the specific area is looking at saving money for Eskom. And if they save money for Eskom by the end of the year they can get bigger bonuses.

Derek
Why are you talking to us?
Evan
Because to go to work on an Eskom power station, it doesn’t matter which one you are working at has actually become a bigger risk than any job, even mining.

Commentary Sixteen
These photos were taken very recently

Evan
They use chain blocks to hold hundreds of kilograms of pipes together.
A chain block doesn’t have any spring support so when the pipe goes down and that chain block breaks it means that the whole pipe is coming down.





Evan source
Now water leaks on the floor and it just piles up. Eskom makes a temporary solution of making a wall out of ash. At the end of the day they just leave it like that- water dams up, makes a small dam and the structures with the water underneath it just stand there, it gets rusted it loses its flexibility and strength

Commentary eighteen
But a lack of maintenance doesn’t necessarily lead to a silo collapse –says Engineer Tony Smith - Chairman of the joint structural division at the South African institute of civil engineers

Tony Smith
In essence with a silo, maintenance issues would not cause this problem -

Commentary twenty
But he also cautions Eskom against rejecting Solidarity’s claims out of hand

Tony Smith
Any owner of any structure should take cognisance of reports that come from people so that we can prevent failures

LINK
Whatever the reason– we have to hand it to Eskom – the grid was on the edge, some called it catastrophic, but with a bit of a Magyver solution they are managing to keep the lights on …for now

Chris Yelland
It is a MacGyver solution but one has to take ones hat off to Eskom they have put together an emergency plan that enables them to keep four out of the six generators running

Commentary Twenty-One
On Friday Eskom’s new CEO was candid with the press

Up sound
The situation at the time looked very dire and we predicted a very dire outlook for the rest of the week

Commentary Twenty-Two
But his team exceeded expectations he says


Tshediso Matona
I really have to say that the team as a collective really performed something next to the miraculous as it were.

Commentary Twenty- Two
And it’s these trucks that are part of the miracle.

Up sound CUP Truck roars

Over 200 trucks a day are manually delivering coal to Majuba

LINK
We are in Amersfoort now about 6 kilometres from Majuba, the trucks just keep coming – one every two minutes and I reckon that can be right

Chris
Eskom have put in this emergency plan that involves 30 dump trucks per hour dumping coal onto mobile conveyers that are bypassing the silos that is one dump every two minutes 24 hours non stop

Commentary Twenty -Three
Do the math’s- over 200 trucks a day carrying 30 tones a truck, at a minimum of R150 a ton for 24 months while Eskom rebuilds the silo – It’s an expensive exercise- but the alternative is a country in the dark.

Up Sound Steve Lennon
I am often asked …make their plans


Commentary Twenty- Four
Despite Eskom’s herculean efforts Moody’s still downgraded South Africa on Thursday- electricity supply was partly to blame. Medupi will take another six months before it produces reliable electricity- SA Ii is still extremely vulnerable. 10 00.

THE END

Deon Well our members say its bad maintenance, preventative maintenance and no maintenance at all LINK Eskom have strenuously denied Solidarity’s claims but we were told by sources that there is a lack of maintenance on several of the power stations Commentary fourteen These screeching rollers under the conveyer belt leading to a silo at Thutuka power station have not been maintained. Evan The rollers grinding metal-to-metal, and that causes vibration to the silo. It runs 24 hours a day so that heat is so excessive! And then if there is a coal spillage ..that is a big fire hazard Commentary fifteen Our source who works at a power station says Eskom incentivize, cost cutting which results in skimping on maintenance. Evan Eskom management of the specific area is looking at saving money for Eskom. And if they save money for Eskom by the end of the year they can get bigger bonuses. Derek Why are you talking to us? Evan Because to go to work on an Eskom power station, it doesn’t matter which one you are working at has actually become a bigger risk than any job, even mining. Commentary Sixteen These photos were taken very recently Evan They use chain blocks to hold hundreds of kilograms of pipes together. A chain block doesn’t have any spring support so when the pipe goes down and that chain block breaks it means that the whole pipe is coming down. Evan source Now water leaks on the floor and it just piles up. Eskom makes a temporary solution of making a wall out of ash. At the end of the day they just leave it like that- water dams up, makes a small dam and the structures with the water underneath it just stand there, it gets rusted it loses its flexibility and strength Commentary eighteen But a lack of maintenance doesn’t necessarily lead to a silo collapse –says Engineer Tony Smith - Chairman of the joint structural division at the South African institute of civil engineers Tony Smith In essence with a silo, maintenance issues would not cause this problem - Commentary twenty But he also cautions Eskom against rejecting Solidarity’s claims out of hand Tony Smith Any owner of any structure should take cognisance of reports that come from people so that we can prevent failures LINK Whatever the reason– we have to hand it to Eskom – the grid was on the edge, some called it catastrophic, but with a bit of a Magyver solution they are managing to keep the lights on …for now Chris Yelland It is a MacGyver solution but one has to take ones hat off to Eskom they have put together an emergency plan that enables them to keep four out of the six generators running Commentary Twenty-One On Friday Eskom’s new CEO was candid with the press Up sound The situation at the time looked very dire and we predicted a very dire outlook for the rest of the week Commentary Twenty-Two But his team exceeded expectations he says Tshediso Matona I really have to say that the team as a collective really performed something next to the miraculous as it were. Commentary Twenty- Two And it’s these trucks that are part of the miracle. Up sound CUP Truck roars Over 200 trucks a day are manually delivering coal to Majuba LINK We are in Amersfoort now about 6 kilometres from Majuba, the trucks just keep coming – one every two minutes and I reckon that can be right Chris Eskom have put in this emergency plan that involves 30 dump trucks per hour dumping coal onto mobile conveyers that are bypassing the silos that is one dump every two minutes 24 hours non stop Commentary Twenty -Three Do the math’s- over 200 trucks a day carrying 30 tones a truck, at a minimum of R150 a ton for 24 months while Eskom rebuilds the silo – It’s an expensive exercise- but the alternative is a country in the dark. Up Sound Steve Lennon I am often asked …make their plans Commentary Twenty- Four Despite Eskom’s herculean efforts Moody’s still downgraded South Africa on Thursday- electricity supply was partly to blame. Medupi will take another six months before it produces reliable electricity- SA Ii is still extremely vulnerable. 10 00. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A crack and then a collapse - can Eskom keep the lights on as it scrambles to fix a collapsed coal silo
metadata.Summary: A ten thousand ton coal silo at Majuba cracked and then collapsed 40 minutes later. Its a setback the country cannot afford. What went wrong - was this just an accident or is Eskoms lack of maintenance catching up with it. In 2008 rolling mass black outs cost thousands of jobs and was a major set back for the economy- are we seeing a repeat of those dark days again?
metadata.Further information: Eskom breaks again Proposal On Saturday around midday Eskom employees noticed a crack in one of Majuba’s coal silos. Less than an hour later this enormous structure had collapsed sending staff into a tailspin and the country into stage 2 load shedding less than 12 hours later. On Sunday the new CEO Tshediso Matona and his team convened a hasty press conference and apologized to the nation. 12 pages of load shedding schedules were released and trucks lined up outside Majuba to deliver coal manually to save South Africa’s grid # Load shedding became the trending topic across TWITTER SA as South Africans in towns and suburbs across the country vented their fury in the dark. By Monday evening Andrew Etzinger Eskom’s Duracell communication man sounded more upbeat and it seemed that although things were bad they were not as catastrophic as Ted Blom had predicted. This release came from the Media desk: Eskom is not load shedding today and does not anticipate that there will be any load shedding tomorrow as additional units have been returned from maintenance. If customers experience power outages during this period, we advise that they contact their electricity providers as it could be a localised problem. The risk of load shedding has reduced significantly and the prognosis for the week is better than expected. The system will be under extreme pressure on Wednesday and Thursday as the water reserves that we built up over the weekend for our peaking plants will be depleted. Eskom is pleased to announce that work at Majuba Power Station has progressed better than anticipated. Teams have worked non-stop since the incident on Saturday and have been able to connect coal feeder units which have enabled us to ramp up the supply from 600MW to 1 200 MW. But that was only on Monday. So what went wrong – Eskom say they will need to do a forensic investigation but Solidarity were less forgiving. On Monday afternoon they released this statement: “Since January, Eskom has been aware of structural problems of the silo which collapsed at its Majuba power station the day before yesterday….Solidarity blames Eskom for not having addressed the issue, accusing the company of negligence. Solidarity has learnt that Eskom workers had been monitoring resonances at the silo since January. It had been reported to the company at that stage that, based on the increase in vibration, the silo was showing signs of deterioration. According to Deon Reyneke, Solidarity’s Head of the Energy Industry, it was found in June this year, and again three weeks prior to the collapse, that the silo’s vibration had worsened. “Vibration of a concrete structure is extremely problematic. The vibration caused or worsened weaknesses in the silo and as the vibration increased, it eventually led to the collapse,” Reyneke explains. But Eskom has disputed this and say that Solidarity has it all wrong. Meanwhile we are told from both inside and outside Eskom that it could take anything from 3 months to a year to fix the problem. Considering that Eskom is battling to keep the lights on without this latest collapse all bets are off on what the country could face in the upcoming summer. Since 2008 there is nothing that angers people more than load- shedding. But anger is one thing – the effects on the economy are dramatic and we simply cannot afford another disaster like this. Azar Jammine explains how this latest Eskom collapse will impact on SA INC.
